idiom_name: mapper free functions or a small mapper class in one translation unit (to_dto / from_dto)
implementation_notes: C++ offers no general converter, so the default is hand-written: free functions in one translation unit - `UserDto to_dto(const User&)` and `User from_dto(const UserDto&)` - or a small mapper class when the conversion needs state (units, locale, configuration). Types do the enforcing: the DTO lives in its own header with no domain includes, `enum class` and `std::optional` carry closed sets and absent values instead of sentinels, and the struct-literal construction of the target makes a newly added field a compile error rather than a silent omission. Conversion operators (`operator User()`) and converting constructors are the alternative C++ form, but implicit conversions widen the call surface with invisible translations, so prefer named functions (mark a constructor `explicit` when you must use one). Use a polymorphic mapper interface only when one caller must target several representations.
pitfalls: A converting constructor or `operator User()` translates implicitly at every call site; invisible conversions are how `User` values appear from unrelated code paths.
The DTO header must not be included by the domain: once it is, the two representations share a compilation dependency and the mapper is decoration.
Returning large DTOs by value relies on copy elision and moves; a mapper that takes and returns by value in a hot loop pays for copies the call site cannot see.
A mapper class with virtuals invites a hierarchy of mappers (one per format); that is a strategy choice, not a free upgrade, and it costs a vtable hop per conversion.

variants.name: JSON ADL serialization hooks (nlohmann::json)
variants.idiom_name: to_json / from_json free functions found by ADL (nlohmann::adl_serializer)
variants.implementation_notes: When the other representation is JSON, the invocation is taken over by the library: declare `void to_json(nlohmann::json&, const User&)` and `void from_json(const nlohmann::json&, User&)` in the type's own namespace and `nlohmann::json j = user;` / `user = j.get<User>()` route through `nlohmann::adl_serializer`, which finds the hooks by argument-dependent lookup. The mapper still decides names, defaults and units; the library only locates and calls it, so keep the hooks next to the type they serve and use `at()` / `value()` deliberately for fields whose absence has meaning. Choose this over a hand-rolled parser whenever the wire format is JSON, and keep explicit mapper functions for the in-memory domain-to-DTO step where no serializer participates.
pitfalls: The hooks must be visible at the point of use and live in the type's namespace; a hook in the wrong namespace is simply not found and the serialization silently falls back to an error or a structural guess.
`json::get<T>()` on an absent key throws, so decide per field between `at()`, `value()` and `contains()` instead of discovering the policy at runtime.
`j.get<User>()` default-constructs the target before filling it: types without a default constructor need a specialization of `adl_serializer` instead of a plain `from_json`.
